nodes.title: 25. 익수
nodes.summary:
The document is a comprehensive field-emergency care standard manual for Korean paramedics, focusing on adult cardiac arrest.  
It details:  
- High-quality chest-compression technique (depth, rate, full recoil, monitoring tools, mechanical devices).  
- Airway management options (OPA, BVM, advanced supraglottic or ETT) with oxygenation and ventilation ratios.  
- Rapid AED use, rhythm checks every 2 min, immediate post-shock CPR.  
- IV epinephrine 1 mg every 3–5 min, fluid bolus, prioritizing compressions/defibrillation over line placement.  
- Special situations: tight spaces, transport CPR, infection control with PPE/HEPA filters, minimal crew exposure.  
- Traumatic arrest protocol: simultaneous search & treatment of reversible causes (5H/5T), hemorrhage control, fluids, needle decompression, pelvic splint, early transport.  
- Documentation, hospital pre-notification, handover of drugs and CPR details.

nodes.title: 26. 전기손상
nodes.summary:
The excerpt is a field-emergency-care protocol for Korean EMTs covering:  
1. Oxygen delivery (15 L/min via NRB/BVM) and airway management (jaw-thrust, BVM, ETT, SGA) tailored to arrest causes (trauma, choking, drowning, OD).  
2. High-quality chest-compression specifics (5 cm depth, 100-120/min, 1:1 duty cycle, mechanical device use in confined/exposure situations).  
3. AED rhythm checks every 2 min/5 cycles, shock delivery workflow, and immediate CPR resumption.  
4. Minimum 6 min on-scene CPR (2020 guidelines + PHTLS), priority trauma care, rapid transport if no ROSC.  
5. Transport-phase CPR monitoring (EtCO₂) and IV access without interrupting compressions.

nodes.title: 27. 일산화탄소 중독
nodes.summary:
The excerpt is a field-emergency CPR protocol for Korean EMS crews.  
Key points:  
- Advanced airway (intubation) must be placed before transport if possible; placement is verified by bilateral chest rise, auscultation, and capnography.  
- Chest compressions continue at 100 min⁻¹ with 10 ventilations min⁻¹ through the advanced airway; no pauses except for defibrillation.  
- AED pads are applied without delaying compressions; rhythm checks every 2 min (5 cycles) with immediate CPR resumption after shock or no-shock advice.  
- Minimum 6 min of high-quality CPR on scene unless trauma-arrest requires immediate intervention; transport starts only after continuous compressions and IV access (if achievable without delay).  
- En-route CPR quality is monitored with capnography; ambulance is not stopped solely for rhythm checks.  
- Receiving hospital is pre-notified; EMS hands over only after hospital CPR is begun and full documentation is completed.  
- Safety: PPE against blood/fluids, seat-belt use, no prolonged pulse check (<10 s), compressions resume instantly post-shock, airway devices left in place even if patient awakens, compressions minimized in narrow elevators.

nodes.title: 28. 기타 화학물질 중독
nodes.summary:
The excerpt outlines key on-scene emergency-care rules for Korean paramedics when managing victims of traumatic cardiac arrest.  
Core points:

1. **Pre-transport coordination**  
   - Phone the receiving hospital before departure to confirm capacity, pass patient/resuscitation data via the fire dispatch center, and ensure uninterrupted CPR.

2. **Continuous resuscitation & hand-over**  
   - Keep CPR, defibrillation and airway management active until hospital staff take over; transmit CPR details to the emergency team; complete the run sheet and trauma-cardiac-arrest form immediately after hand-over.

3. **Specific on-scene/transport safety and treatment notes**  
   - Wear PPE (traffic and infection risk).  
   - Start CPR if pulse uncertain after ≤10 s.  
   - Compress immediately after every shock, ignore "no-shock-advised" tones for the full 2-min cycle; leave AED ON and patches attached unless patient movement truly demands it.  
   - Do not interrupt compressions to "check" the patient unless you see ROSC signs (movement, coughing, ECG, EtCO₂ spike).  
   - Leave advanced airways (OPA/NPA/ETT) in place even if consciousness returns unless clear gag and medical direction allows removal.  
   - Minimise chest-compression pauses in cramped elevators; maintain patient position to preserve circulation.

4. **Reference list (provided) cites 2015-23 international and Korean trauma-resuscitation sources covering massive transfusion, needle decompression for tension pneumothorax, and pre-hospital resuscitative strategy.

nodes.title: 31. 소생 후 치료
nodes.summary:
The excerpt is a field-treatment protocol manual for Korean EMTs.  
It gives step-by-step standard guidelines for four critical conditions:

1. Post-resuscitation care – how to manage a patient who has achieved ROSC (airway, oxygenation, vitals monitoring, fluid bolus, prevention of re-arrest, transport destination).  
2. Non-traumatic shock – early recognition by altered mental status, skin, pulse, respiration; differentiation of hypovolemic, cardiogenic, neurogenic, septic and anaphylactic shock; mandatory history points, vital-sign reference table, high-flow O₂, IV fluid strategy, positioning, warming, transport rules.  
3. Foreign-body airway obstruction – distinction between partial vs complete block; encourage cough, back blows, abdominal thrusts (chest thrusts in pregnancy/obesity), CPR if unconscious, finger sweep only when object seen, warnings against blind sweeps and oral intake, transport criteria.  
4. Dyspnea – ventilation/perfusion/diffusion framework; characteristic features of asthma, COPD, heart failure/pulmonary edema, spontaneous pneumothorax; OPQRST history, AVPU/vitals/physical exam checklist; O₂ delivery algorithms (target SpO₂ 88-98 % depending on disease), nebulized bronchodilators, CPAP, CPAP cautions in pneumothorax, indications for advanced airway, transport hospital selection.

Each section ends with precautions, criteria for on-line medical direction, and hospital-destination rules (nearest appropriate emergency facility, with regional exceptions).

nodes.title: 32. 산소 투여
nodes.summary:
The excerpt is a field-emergency protocol for Korean paramedics.  
It first lists target oxygen-saturation ranges (88–98 %) for major adult conditions such as acute severe illness, COPD, AMI, ARDS, major trauma, and post-ROSC patients, noting that 100 % O₂ is reserved for specific situations (chest trauma, drowning, airway burns, CO poisoning, anaphylaxis, etc.).  
The second half details “hyperventilation syndrome”: typical profile (young women, stress-triggered), clinical features (progressive dyspnea, fear, carpopedal spasm, dizziness), essential assessment points (history, ruling out serious mimics), and step-by-step prehospital care (standard initial evaluation, SpO₂ monitoring, O₂ via face-mask only if SpO₂ < 94 %, and coaching slow breathing until handover).

nodes.title: 33. 과호흑
nodes.summary:
The excerpt is a field-emergency protocol (Part 3-Ⅰ) on “hyperventilation syndrome.”  
It defines the condition as excessive unconscious rapid breathing that lowers arterial CO₂, lists its typical presentation (young women, gradual dyspnea, fear, carpopedal spasm, dizziness), and stresses ruling out life-threatening mimics (PE, MI).  
Core on-scene actions: follow standard initial assessment, monitor SpO₂, give 6–10 L/min O₂ only if SpO₂ < 94%, coach slow breathing, avoid re-breathing bags, continuously monitor vitals/ECG, and transport to the nearest appropriate emergency facility while considering direct medical direction.

nodes.title: 34. 흉통
nodes.summary:
The excerpt is a field-emergency protocol (Part 3-Ⅰ) for Korean EMTs covering two core topics:

1. Cardiac-origin chest pain  
   - Distinguishes stable angina from acute myocardial infarction (STEMI vs NSTEMI)  
   - Lists typical/atypical presentations, obligatory patient-history items (OPQRST, risk factors, PDE-5 inhibitor use), vital-sign & 12-lead ECG assessment, oxygen and nitroglycerin dosing rules, IV access, CPAP for suspected cardiogenic pulmonary edema, contraindications, on-line medical-control triggers, and destination criteria (PCI-capable hospital for STEMI, otherwise nearest appropriate emergency center)

2. Symptomatic bradycardia  
   - Defines bradycardia (<60 bpm) and “relative” bradycardia, stressing perfusion-related red-flag symptoms (altered mentation, hypotension, chest pain, dyspnea, syncope, heart failure)  
   - Mandates airway/oxygenation, history for precipitants/drugs, vital-sign monitoring, and 3-lead ECG when available

nodes.title: 35. 서맥
nodes.summary:
The excerpt is a field-treatment protocol for Korean EMTs covering two arrhythmias:

1. Bradycardia (서맥) – defines slow heart rate (< 60 bpm, usually symptomatic < 50 bpm), distinguishes “relative” bradycardia, lists critical signs (altered mental status, hypotension, chest pain, dyspnea, syncope, CHF, shock), outlines causes (vagal tone, conduction blocks, drugs, ischemia), mandatory assessment points (history, vitals, 3-lead ECG), step-by-step care (airway/oxygen, IV if unstable, continuous monitoring), precautions (rule-out PEA, MI), and transport criteria (regional emergency center or higher, call medical command if unstable).

2. Tachycardia (빈맥) – defines fast heart rate (≥ 100 bpm, usually symptomatic ≥ 150 bpm), classifies narrow vs wide QRS, lists identical critical signs, assessment steps, initial management (airway/oxygen, monitor, 3-lead ECG), and transport considerations.

nodes.title: 36. 빈맥
nodes.summary:
The excerpt is the “Field Emergency-Care Standard Guideline” section on tachycardia and syncope.  
For tachycardia (HR ≥ 100 bpm, usually symptomatic ≥ 150 bpm) it explains:  
- Classification into narrow- vs wide-QRS types  
- Red-flag symptoms (altered mentation, hypotension, chest pain, dyspnea, syncope, CHF, sweating, N/V)  
- Mandatory patient work-up (history, vitals, pulse check, 3-lead ECG, SpO₂)  
- Step-by-step pre-hospital care (airway/oxygen, monitoring, defibrillation if VT/VF, IV access)  
- Caveats (pulseless wide-QRS → cardiac-arrest protocol; rule out MI)  
- When to request on-line medical direction and how to choose the receiving hospital (regional EMC or higher, unless unstable).  

For syncope (sudden, transient loss of consciousness from global cerebral hypoperfusion) it covers:  
- Key differential (cardiogenic, hypovolemic shock, stroke, vasovagal, situational, orthostatic, hypoglycemia, hypoxia, drug toxicity)  
- Prodromal symptoms that distinguish it from seizure  
- Essential assessment points (history of cardiac syncope, associated symptoms, event details, recurrence, medications)

nodes.title: 37. 실신
nodes.summary:
The excerpt is a field-treatment protocol for Korean EMTs covering two emergencies:

1. Syncope (실신) – Defines it as sudden, transient loss of consciousness from transient cerebral hypoperfusion; lists cardiogenic, hypovolemic, vasovagal, situational, orthostatic, hypoglycemic, hypoxic, toxic causes; emphasizes distinguishing it from seizure and identifying life-threatening forms. Details mandatory patient assessment (history, vitals, SpO₂, blood glucose, 3-lead ECG) and step-by-step pre-hospital care: airway/oxygen (nasal cannula 1–5 L/min or face-mask 6–10 L/min, upgrade to non-rebreather 11–15 L/min if SpO₂ < 95%), IV access with 300 mL crystalloid (up to 1 L) for shock, safety precautions against falls or cervical/head injury, nil per os if alert, and transport to an emergency-capable hospital when cardiogenic or hypovolemic syncope is suspected.

2. Hemoptysis (객혈) – Characterized as expectoration of bright-red, frothy blood from lower airway disease; common causes bronchitis, TB, bronchiectasis, pneumonia, lung abscess, cancer. Defines massive hemoptysis (100–600 mL/24 h or ≥150 mL/h) and risk of asphyxiation. Required evaluation: history of pulmonary disease, anticoagulants, prior hemoptysis, amount/duration, plus vital-sign survey for shock (SBP < 90 mmHg, tachycardia/bradycardia, tachypnea, SpO₂, fever) and chest auscultation to localize disease.

nodes.summary:

It defines each type of bleeding, lists common causes, emphasizes rapid differentiation, details the essential history and physical exam (including shock/airway assessment, vital-sign thresholds, oxygen saturation, estimated bleeding rate), and gives step-by-step emergency measures: airway maintenance, oxygen delivery algorithms, fluid resuscitation volumes, advanced airway indications, precautions during transport, criteria for on-line medical direction, and destination-hospital selection rules.

nodes.title: 39. 토혈/혈변
nodes.summary:

It defines the two conditions, lists key history and exam items (amount of bleeding, shock signs, stigmata of liver disease), gives step-by-step pre-hospital care (airway protection, oxygen to keep SpO₂ ≥ 94 %, lateral positioning to prevent aspiration, IV access and crystalloid for SBP < 90 mmHg or shock), stresses bringing collected blood/stool to hospital, states when to request on-line medical direction, and specifies that massive bleeds or cirrhotic variceal rupture should go to the nearest regional emergency center.

nodes.title: 40. 대사성 의식 장애
nodes.summary:
Korean field-emergency guideline “Part Ⅰ” on metabolic consciousness disorders.
Key contents:
- Definition/pathophysiology of metabolic coma (non-traumatic CNS hypo-responsiveness)
- AVPU scale (A=Alert, V=Verbal, P=Pain-responsive, U=Unresponsive)
- Causative classes: hypoxia/ischemia, hypoglycaemia, vitamin deficit, organ failure, toxins/drugs, infections, epilepsy-post-ictal, acid-base or ionic imbalance
- Clinical pearls: abnormal vitals may be both consequence and cause; fever suggests infection
Patient-assessment checklist:
- Collateral history (baseline diseases, current drugs, scene circumstances)
- Vital signs, SpO₂, temperature, capillary glucose, AVPU grade, pupil reactions, pain-induced motor asymmetry, pathological reflexes, ECG, incontinence/tongue-biting for seizure risk
Emergency steps:
- Standard primary survey; lay patient flat with head-up tilt if SBP ≥ 90 mmHg to protect airway; suction/airway adjunct if gag reflex lost; high-flow O₂ via facemask if AVPU≤V and SpO₂<94%

nodes.title: 41. 응급분만
nodes.summary:
The excerpt is a field-treatment protocol for Korean paramedics managing an unconscious or altered-consciousness patient.  
Main points:  
1. Mandatory patient assessment: gather history from bystanders, check vitals (BP, RR, HR, SpO₂, temp, glucose), use AVPU for consciousness, evaluate pupils, pain response, movement, reflexes, ECG, and signs of seizure.  
2. Initial care sequence: follow “Initial Patient Evaluation & Treatment Guideline”; position patient (head-up 15–30° if SBP ≥ 90 mmHg); secure airway if gag reflex absent; give 6–10 L/min O₂ by face mask (AVPU = V, SpO₂ < 94 %) or 11–15 L/min via BVM/NRM plus assisted ventilation (AVPU = P/U, SpO₂ < 94 %).  
3. Immediate dextrose: if bedside glucose ≤ 70 mg/dL, start IV and give 50 mL 50 % dextrose (children: 5 mL/kg 10 %).  
4. Precautions: nothing by mouth, do not delay transport for neuro exams, cool hyperthermic patients, monitor vitals/ECG en route.  
5. Indications for on-line medical direction: unstable vitals needing IV fluids, hypoglycaemia requiring dextrose, prolonged transport (>1 h) with inadequate ventilation, or suspected cardiovascular cause of altered consciousness.  
6. Destination policy: AVPU = P/U patients → nearest regional emergency centre; in underserved areas → closest capable facility; if uncertain, request medical direction.

nodes.title: 42. 급성 뇌졸중의증
nodes.summary:
The excerpt is the “Field Emergency Care Standard Guideline” for suspected acute stroke.  
It classifies stroke (ischemic vs. hemorrhagic), lists risk factors and typical symptoms, then details the pre-hospital workflow:  
1) Mandatory patient assessment—last-normal time, symptom course, past history, vital signs, AVPU, pupil/motor exams, CPSS and CSTAT stroke scales, ECG.  
2) Step-by-step care—positioning, airway/oxygen, glucose check with dextrose for <70 mg/dL, continuous monitoring.  
3) Key precautions—no oral intake, avoid delays, no field blood-pressure control, 6-hour window for thrombectomy-capable hospital, ≤10 min on-scene.  
4) Criteria for on-line medical direction and choice of receiving hospital (regional emergency center or higher, thrombolysis-ready if CPSS positive).

nodes.title: 43. 경련
nodes.summary:

It defines seizure/epilepsy/status epilepticus, lists age-specific causes, describes typical prodromal and post-ictal signs, then details pre-hospital assessment (history from bystanders, vitals, glucose, AVPU, pupils, pain response, ECG) and step-by-step care for both actively convulsing and post-ictal patients (airway protection, O₂ if SpO₂ < 94%, dextrose 50 % 50 mL IV if glucose ≤ 70 mg/dL, positioning, safety measures, contraindications).  
It gives criteria for on-line medical direction, choice of receiving hospital (nearest capable facility, obstetric capability if pregnant), and adds a parallel protocol for acute hypoglycemia: confirm with glucometer, give oral glucose if alert, IV 10 % dextrose if not, followed by maintenance drip.

nodes.title: 44. 급성 저혈당 의증
nodes.summary:
The excerpt is the field-emergency standard protocol for “suspected acute hypoglycemia” (Chapter 259).  
It defines the condition (adults <70 mg/dL, children <60 mg/dL plus altered mental status, diaphoresis, seizure, unconsciousness), lists rapid assessment items (history of missed meals, overdose of diabetic drugs, increased activity; physical findings of tremor, pallor, tachycardia, sweating), and gives a step-by-step treatment algorithm: confirm with glucometer, give oral glucose 25–50 g if alert, establish IV and give 10 % or 50 % dextrose (5 mL/kg or 50 mL) if not alert, follow with 10 % dextrose drip, re-check glucose every 30–60 min, suction vomitus, watch for meter error, consider stroke/trauma/seizure/cardiac arrest if no response, request on-line medical direction when unstable or persistent unconsciousness, and transport to the nearest appropriate emergency facility based on response and suspected alternate causes.

nodes.title: 45. 발열 및 패혈증성 쇼크
nodes.summary:
The excerpt is the “Fever & Septic Shock” chapter of the Korean EMS “Field Emergency Care Standard Guideline.”  
It defines normal vs. febrile body temperature, lists major causes (infection, rheumatologic disease, malignancy), and details the progression from SIRS through sepsis, severe sepsis to septic shock.  
It gives EMS crews mandatory assessment items (history red-flags, physical findings), step-by-step field treatment (tepid sponging for simple fever; high-flow O₂, IV access, 300 mL–1 L crystalloid for sepsis/shock), safety rules (infection control, PPE, post-exposure prophylaxis), criteria for on-line medical direction, and destination-hospital selection based on severity and regional resources.

nodes.title: 46. 알레르기 및 아나필락시스
nodes.summary:
The excerpt is the field-treatment protocol for two emergency conditions—anaphylaxis and abnormal-behavior/suicide attempts—taken from the Korean “Standard First-Aid Guidelines for EMTs.”  
For anaphylaxis it defines the disorder, lists common triggers (drugs, insect venom), distinguishes mild allergy from life-threatening anaphylaxis, gives diagnostic criteria (≥2-organ involvement or isolated hypotension after known exposure), details step-by-step care (remove allergen, high-flow O₂, airway management, IV fluid bolus, intramuscular epinephrine auto-injector use, repeat dosing, precautions in cardiovascular disease), and specifies when to request on-line medical direction and to transport to an emergency medical center.  
For abnormal behavior/suicide it stresses scene safety first, outlines possible causes (psychiatric illness, substance abuse, medical disorders), mandatory assessment points (psychiatric history, threat to self/others, co-existing trauma/intoxication/hypoglycaemia), red-flag signs (hallucinations, delusions, agitation, self-harm), and the need to look for underlying medical causes, treat associated injuries or poisoning, and notify police when suicide is suspected.

nodes.title: 47. 행동 이상 및 자살
nodes.summary:

It defines abnormal behavior/suicide, lists clinical features (agitation, hallucinations, self-harm, etc.), details mandatory on-scene assessments (psychiatric history, co-existing trauma/intoxication, hypoglycaemia check), and gives a step-by-step care algorithm: secure scene → verbal de-escalation → vital-sign/glucose check → treat hypoglycaemia/trauma/intoxication → collect suicide-method data.  
It specifies when and how to request police assistance, how police, fire and mental-health centres share roles, how to document every interaction, criteria for direct medical consultation, patient-refusal / non-transport rules, and destination-hospital selection (nearest psychiatric facility, administrative admission routes, or tele-consult in underserved areas).

nodes.title: 48. 응급 분만

nodes.title: 49. 질출혈

nodes.title: 51. 자간증
nodes.summary:
The excerpt is a field-treatment protocol manual for Korean EMTs.  
It gives step-by-step guidance for the pre-hospital management of:

1. Obstetric emergency: eclampsia – history points, BP thresholds, seizure care (airway, O₂, left-lateral tilt, IV access), post-partum vigilance, and mandatory delivery-capable hospital transport.  
2. Neonatal resuscitation – rapid assessment (term? crying? tone?), pulse check, ventilation first, 3:1 compression:ventilation ratio, start with 21 % O₂ for ≥35 wk, thermoregulation, meconium suction before shoulder delivery, epinephrine & airway indications, transport to neonatal-ready facility.  
3. Infant/child cardiac arrest – asphyxial aetiology predominates, 2-min CPR cycles, 100-120 compressions min⁻¹ (1/3 chest depth), 15:2 or 30:2 ratio, 2 J kg⁻¹ → 4 J kg⁻¹ defibrillation, epi 0.01 mg kg⁻¹ IV/IO, Broselow tape weight, airway 10-20 breaths min⁻¹, 5H-5T reversible causes.  
4. Paediatric foreign-body airway – partial vs complete obstruction, back blows / chest thrusts (age-specific), Heimlich ≥1 yr, no blind finger sweep, Magill forceps if visible, CPR if unconscious, mandatory hospital follow-up.  
5. Child respiratory distress – age/seasonal differentials (bronchiolitis, asthma, croup, epiglottitis), signs of increased work, O₂ by blow-by or BVM, SpO₂ targets, nebuliser indications, transport to paediatric-capable centre.  
6. Paediatric seizures – febrile vs non-febrile, status epilepticus definition, protect airway, O₂, check glucose, no forced oral meds, IV access, rectal diazepam if available, transport for IV anticonvulsants.  
7. Paediatric fever – define significant temperature by age, assess vaccination history, look for serious bacterial infection markers, remove excess clothing, transport high-risk infants (<3 mo, preterm, chronic disease).  
8. Major trauma – physiological & anatomic criteria for “severe/multisystem” label, <10 min scene time, airway with cervical spine control, bleeding control, 2 large-bore IVs, 300 mL–1 L crystalloid, maintain SpO₂ 96-98%, prevent hypothermia, pain score ≥8 → IV acetaminophen (15 min infusion), log-roll transfers, direct medical oversight for bypass/destination decisions, prefer regional trauma centre, helicopter criteria (>30 km or >1 h ground), repeated vitals en-route.

nodes.title: 머리 손상
nodes.summary:
The excerpt is a field-treatment protocol for Korean EMTs covering two major trauma categories:

1. Head injury  
   - Definition and classification (scalp, skull, brain; mild vs. severe).  
   - Key clinical warnings: occult bleeding / delayed symptoms possible.  
   - Mandatory on-scene assessment: history from patient/bystander, AVPU/GCS, pupillary & motor checks, vitals q5 min, palpation for depressed skull fracture or posterior-neck tenderness.  
   - Step-by-step care: airway opening (OPA/NPA, avoid NPA if skull fracture suspected), O₂ to keep SpO₂ ≥ 94 %, 30° head-up if ↑ICP signs, C-collar & spinal motion restriction for all severe cases, fluid bolus 300 mL–1 L for SBP < 90 mmHg, pressure dressing for external bleeding, continuous monitoring.  
   - Time limit: ≤ 10 min on-scene for severe cases; watch for airway compromise from vomiting/facial injury.  
   - Direct medical direction required for CPR decisions, IV access, unclear severity, or transport dilemmas.  
   - Transport rules: severe → regional trauma center; mild & stable → nearest local ED; helicopter if ground transport clearly slower.

2. Spinal & spinal-cord injury  
   - Mechanisms: blunt, penetrating, distraction, high-speed crashes, falls > 1 m / 5 steps, diving, bicycle/motorcycle crashes.  
   - Clinical picture: motor/sensory deficit below level, spinal shock (flaccid paralysis, hypotension, bradycardia), later autonomic dysreflexia.  
   - Assessment: same rapid trauma survey (airway, AVPU, vitals) plus focused history of high-risk mechanism and neurologic deficits.  
   - Implicit treatment: maintain airway, spinal immobilization, monitor vitals, transport to appropriate facility.

nodes.title: 비뇨생식기 손상
nodes.summary:
The excerpt is a field-treatment protocol for emergency-medical technicians on “genitourinary trauma.”  
Main points:  
1. Definition: external-force injuries to kidneys, bladder, genitals (males: even penile amputation).  
2. Clinical clues: vague complaints; suspect renal injury with lower-rib/flank/upper-abdomen trauma; suspect bladder/urethral injury with pelvic fractures.  
3. Mandatory assessment: mechanism, pregnancy/medication history, airway-breathing-circulation check, look for flank/pelvic bruising or blood at urethral meatus.  
4. Treatment sequence: standard trauma airway; O₂ if SpO₂ < 94%; 18 G IV, 300 mL–1 L crystalloid for SBP < 90 mmHg; spinal/pelvic immobilization; manage amputated penis (saline-moist gauze, cold storage).  
5. Time limit: ≤ 10 min on-scene for severe cases; watch for associated injuries and possible sexual assault.  
6. Indications for on-line medical direction: CPR decisions, IV access, amputation care, uncertain severity.  
7. Destination rules: severe cases → regional trauma center; mild cases → nearest EMT-level hospital; helicopter if ground transport > ~15 min.

nodes.title: 치과적 손상
nodes.summary:
The excerpt is a field-treatment protocol for dental trauma aimed at Korean EMTs.  
Main points:  
1. Definition and types – fractures, luxation, avulsion, soft-tissue injuries.  
2. Clinical pearls – often co-exists with facial/head injury; >60 % from falls or sports; avulsed tooth may be aspirated.  
3. Mandatory on-scene assessment – history (time of avulsion, mechanism, past medical history), airway/breathing check, vital signs, intra-oral inspection for fragments/bleeding/foreign bodies, look for associated injuries.  
4. Emergency care steps – follow general trauma guideline, handle avulsed tooth only by crown, store in milk/physiologic saline, apply pressure dressing for soft-tissue bleeding.  
5. Precautions – limit scene time to <10 min if severe trauma, protect loose teeth during airway maneuvers, do not re-implant primary teeth unless uncertain, suspect child abuse in pediatric cases.  
6. Indications for on-line medical direction – heavily contaminated tooth, unclear severity, difficult treatment decisions.  
7. Destination rules – severe cases → regional trauma center or dental university hospital; mild isolated cases → nearest facility capable of dental trauma care; remote areas → closest available dental-capable hospital.

nodes.title: 화상
nodes.summary:
The excerpt is a field-triage chapter from Korea’s “Environmental Emergency Care Standard Guidelines.”  
It gives pre-hospital crews a rapid, step-by-step protocol for two specific injuries:

1. Burns  
   - Scene safety first; classify burns by agent (thermal, electrical, chemical, radiation) and depth (1°, 2°, 3°).  
   - Lists skin-function loss, clinical appearance, pain, blistering, healing time and red-flag criteria (≥5 % 3°, ≥20 % 2°, face/hands/genitalia involvement, inhalation, associated trauma).  
   - Mandatory assessments: airway for inhalation injury (singed hairs, soot, stridor, wheeze), burn size (Rule of Nines or palm method), associated injuries.  
   - Treatment sequence: high-flow 100 % O₂ for every fire-scene patient, airway adjuncts or intubation if GCS ≤P, RR ≥30 or SpO₂ <90 %, 18 G IV access with 500 mL lactated Ringer’s q5–10 min until normotensive, cool running water then dry sterile wrap, remove jewellery/clothes, avoid ice.  
   - Time limit: ≤10 min on-scene for critical burns; do not delay transport for lines.  
   - Destination rules: isolated major burn → nearest regional ED or burn centre; combined trauma → direct medical consultation; if ground transport >helicopter time, request air lift.

2. Electrical & lightning injuries  
   - Pathophysiology: entry/exit wounds, deep muscle necrosis, fractures from tetany, arrhythmias; lightning may cause asystole/respiratory arrest and fern-like skin marks (Lichtenberg figures).  
   - History: voltage, AC/DC, pathway, exposure time; exam: continuous ECG monitoring, look for fall injuries.  
   - Same airway algorithm as above; intubate if indicated.

Throughout, the text stresses early oxygenation, rapid volume resuscitation, prevention of hypothermia, minimal scene time, and immediate direct medical guidance or specialist-centre transfer when criteria are met.

2. Mandatory patient assessment – voltage/type of current, body pathway, exposure time, past history; ECG monitoring and search for associated trauma.  
3. Step-by-step pre-hospital care – scene safety, airway management (OPA/NPA, intubation criteria), spinal immobilization, IV access with lactated Ringer’s, fluid resuscitation for shock, CPR for cardiac arrest, fracture splinting, wound dressing, AED standby.  
4. Safety warnings – do not approach until power is off, treat cardiac-arrest victims first in multi-casualty lightning incidents.  
5. Indications for on-line medical direction – need for intubation, IV/fluids, arrhythmias, unclear severity.  
6. Transport rules – nearest regional emergency center or burn-specialty hospital; helicopter requested if faster than ground.

Key points:  
- Defines submersion (immersion with respiratory distress) and drowning (progression to hypoxia and cardiac arrest), noting both “wet” and “dry” mechanisms.  
- Details essential patient assessment: history (duration, water type, temperature, trauma risk) and physical findings (responsiveness, breathing, consciousness, vomiting, cough).  
- Provides step-by-step pre-hospital management: safe rescue, initial evaluation, removal of wet clothes, airway opening, oxygenation/ventilation (bag-valve mask or advanced airway), high-quality chest compressions (30:2 or continuous with 10 vent/min), AED use, and rewarming for hypothermic arrest.  
- Emphasises spinal motion restriction when trauma is suspected, continuous resuscitation until core temperature ≥35 °C, and mandatory transport even for mild symptoms because of delayed aspiration pneumonia risk.  
- Lists indications for on-line medical direction (resuscitation decisions, advanced airway, IV access, destination choice) and directs transport to the nearest appropriate emergency facility.

1. Hypothermia (pages 378-382)  
   - Definition: core temperature ≤ 35 °C measured with tympanic thermometer.  
   - Clinical grades: mild (≥ 34 °C – shivering, confusion), moderate (30–34 °C – reduced shivering, falling vitals), severe (< 30 °C – no shivering, coma, risk of arrhythmia/cardiac arrest).  
   - Mandatory on-scene assessment: history (thyroid disease, medications, alcohol, exposure time), wet clothing, infection, mental status, slow pulse check (≥ 20 s).  
   - Treatment sequence: remove wet clothes, wrap in dry blankets, protect from further cold; if pulseless/apnoeic follow hypothermic arrest protocol – continuous CPR, airway with OP airway or advanced airway, 10–15 L O₂, BVM ventilation (30:2 or 10/min post-ETT), AED/defibrillation as indicated.  
   - Transport rewarming: maximise cabin heater, apply warm IV bags to axilla/groin (towel-wrapped), monitor vitals/SpO₂.  
   - Cautions: gentle handling to avoid arrhythmias; if no obvious death signs, always start/continue CPR; request on-line medical direction for CPR decisions, advanced airway, IV access, hospital choice.  
   - Destination rule: moderate/severe (< 34 °C) or arrest → regional emergency centre; mild (≥ 34 °C) → nearest local ED.

2. Heat-related illness (page 383)  
   - Populations at risk: elderly, children, poor socio-economic status, dehydration, alcohol/drug abuse, workers in heat, cardiovascular or thyroid disease.  
   - Syndromes:  
     – Heat stroke: thermoregulatory failure, core ≥ 40 °C, CNS dysfunction (confusion, seizures, coma), hot dry skin, tachycardia, hypotension.  
     – Heat exhaustion: dehydration/electrolyte loss, temperature normal-40 °C, headache, dizziness, weakness, vomiting, syncope, sweating persists.  
     – Heat cramps: painful involuntary muscle contractions from salt loss, normal temperature.  
     – Heat syncope: orthostatic faint on sudden heat exposure, rapid recovery.  
     – Heat oedema: peripheral swelling in hot weather.

nodes.title: 고온 환경 질환
nodes.summary:
The excerpt is a field-triage section of Korea’s “Environmental Emergency Care Standard Guidelines.”  
It systematically covers two major topics:

1. Heat-related illness  
   - Defines the spectrum (heat stroke, heat exhaustion, heat cramps, heat syncope, heat edema) and lists predisposing factors.  
   - Gives key clinical findings for each entity, stressing that heat stroke presents with core temperature ≥ 40 °C and altered mental status.  
   - Details mandatory on-scene assessment points: history (age, drugs, exposure time, activity, hydration), AVPU consciousness scale, core temperature, skin condition, vital signs, capillary refill, blood pressure, and point-of-care glucose.  
   - Provides step-by-step pre-hospital treatment: remove from heat, strip clothing, airway/oxygen management, cooling (water + fan, ice packs to axilla/groin, stop if shivering), IV crystalloid 300 mL (up to 1 L if shocked), dextrose for hypoglycaemia, elevate edematous limbs, continuous monitoring, and selective transport to the nearest appropriate emergency facility (regional emergency medical center for suspected heat stroke).

2. Poisoning  
   - Notes common exposure routes and the need to consider hypoxia, opioid toxicity, hypoglycaemia, Wernicke encephalopathy in altered patients.  
   - Summarises toxidromes and antidotes for major poison classes:  
     – Opioids (miosis, respiratory depression) → naloxone.  
     – Sympathomimetics (cocaine, amphetamines: agitation, dilated pupils, tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia, seizures) → supportive care.  
     – Cholinergics (organophosphates/carbamates: SLUDGE, fasciculations) → atropine + 2-PAM.  
     – Acetaminophen (delayed hepatic injury) → N-acetylcysteine.  
     – Tricyclic antidepressants (seizures, arrhythmias, wide QRS) → sodium bicarbonate.  

Throughout, the text uses numbered steps, icons (☞ Ⓕ ② ①) that link to other guideline sections, and explicit criteria for requesting direct medical direction and choosing destination hospitals.

nodes.title: 중독
nodes.summary:
The excerpt is a field-triage chapter titled “Environmental Emergency Care Standard Guideline – Poisoning.”  
It systematically covers:

- Definition, routes and circumstances of poisoning (occupational, environmental, recreational, criminal).  
- Toxidrome-based clinical profiles for major poison classes (opioids, sympathomimetics, organophosphates/carbamates, acetaminophen, TCAs, cardiac drugs, sedatives-hypnotics, hypoglycaemics, paraquat, CO, corrosives) with expected signs, complications and specific antidotes.  
- Bedside evaluation checklist: focused history (agent, dose, time, intent, witnesses, scene clues) and targeted physical exam (airway, breathing, circulation, pupils, skin, secretions, abdomen, neuromuscular status).  
- Step-by-step pre-hospital management: universal precautions & decontamination, airway opening, oxygen strategies (high-flow for CO, withhold for paraquat unless respiratory failure), shock management with fluids, monitoring during transport.  
- Safety rules: PPE, no forced emesis, aspiration prevention.  
- Indications for on-line medical direction (IV access, fluids, glucose, advanced airway, hospital-selection dilemmas).  
- Destination criteria: severity-based triage to regional emergency centres, antidote availability, psychiatric co-capability for suicidal cases, geographic contingency for underserved areas.  
- Quick-reference table matching common poisons to their antidotes.  
- Colour-coding standards for pesticide containers and toxicity labels.

nodes.title: 동물/곤충/뱀 교상/해양동물
nodes.summary:
The excerpt is a field-treatment protocol for Korean EMTs on bites and stings from arthropods (insects, spiders, crustaceans), snakes, land animals, and marine creatures.  
It lists typical local and systemic reactions (pain, edema, anaphylaxis, shock, DIC, etc.), required patient assessment items (history, wound inspection, infection/anaphylaxis screen), step-by-step pre-hospital care (washing, bleeding control, limb immobilization, elastic bandage for snake bite, warm-water immersion for fish stings, IV fluid for hypotension), critical precautions (no ice on snake bites, card removal for bee stingers, avoid rubbing marine stings), and transport rules: direct severe or anaphylactic cases to a regional emergency center, request medical direction for antivenom, while mild local-reaction cases may go to the nearest appropriate facility.

nodes.title: Ⅴ. 특수상황 응급처치 표준지침
nodes.summary: The excerpt outlines the standard emergency-care protocol for mass-casualty and disaster incidents in South Korea. It defines a “mass-casualty incident,” then presents a step-by-step flowchart that 119 rescue teams follow: disaster notification → on-scene arrival and set-up of a temporary treatment post → initial triage (M-MASS) → secondary triage and emergency care (START) → patient transport while tracking hospital capacity → final confirmation of casualty status and disaster termination.

nodes.title: 다수환자 발생 및 재난사고
nodes.summary:
The document is a detailed Korean emergency-care standard for mass-casualty incidents (MCI) and disasters.  
It defines an MCI, outlines the 119-ambulance response flow from alarm to stand-down, and then concentrates on the “임시의료소” (temporary medical post) that first-arriving crews must establish before a full field hospital arrives.  

Core points covered:  
- Purpose and legal definition of the temporary post: command, triage, treatment and transport coordination.  
- When and where to set it up (outside inner cordon, safe, visible, utilities available, weather-proof, separate decedent area).  
- Leadership: qualifications and duties of the temporary post commander (senior EMT, ambulance officer or IC-designate).  
- Modular organisation: Triage, Treatment, Transport teams; staffing and tasking of each team leader.  
- Two-step triage algorithm: 1st-stage Modified MASS (ambulant vs non-ambulant), 2nd-stage START (RPM + airway check).  
- Colour-coded triage tags (or electronic equivalent) and re-triage rules.  
- Treatment priorities: life-threatening first, psychological support for non-urgent; documentation for hospital selection.  
- Transport priorities: urgent > emergent > non-urgent > deceased; 119 ambulances reserved for urgent cases, others for remainder; real-time bed availability via EMS control centre.  
- Decedent management: withhold CPR unless ordered, temporary morgue, evidence preservation, police/family liaison.  
- Phased escalation: 1-ambulance (combined team) → 2-ambulance (split triage/transport) → 3-ambulance (full 3-team post) with flexible staffing and multiple posts if area is large.  
- Adaptations for limited resources, gradual vs sudden patient surge, and confined vs widespread scenes.

nodes.title: 아동학대
nodes.summary:
The excerpt is a field-triage manual section on two special populations—abused children and elderly trauma patients.  
For suspected child abuse it defines abuse/neglect, lists red-flag histories (delayed EMS call, inconsistent stories, developmentally impossible mechanisms), details the head-to-toe skin exam (pattern bruises, geometric burns, bite marks, symmetrical injuries), mandates evidence documentation, prohibits on-scene confrontation, obliges 112 police/physician notification, and designates Sunflower Centers for sexual-abuse cases.  
For elderly patients it notes high fragility, polypharmacy, sensory/cognitive barriers, emphasizes that standard ABC priorities apply, highlights hip and pelvic fractures plus occult brain/intrathoracic injury after falls, and warns that shock may present without typical hypotension/tachycardia after motor-vehicle crashes.

nodes.title: 노인환자
nodes.summary:
The excerpt is a field-triage chapter from Korea’s emergency medical-services “Special-situation first-aid standard.”  
It gives paramedics age-specific protocols for two groups:

1. Elderly patients  
   - Highlights their high fragility, poly-pharmacy, sensory/communication limits and atypical shock or MI presentation.  
   - Details injury patterns: falls (hip/pelvis/proximal-femur fractures), motor-vehicle crashes (cervical-spine, occult shock), head trauma (anticoagulant-related bleeding), plus mandatory spine immobilization.  
   - Covers common medical emergencies—syncope, acute confusion, “silent” chest pain, tachypnea, acute abdomen—and the need to suspect elder abuse/neglect, document evidence discreetly, request on-line medical direction, and choose appropriate trauma or regional emergency center.

2. Sexual-assault patients  
   - Defines sexual violence broadly (any non-consensual sexual contact).  
   - Instructs crews to obtain only minimal, non-judgemental history in the victim’s own words, avoid genital exam unless life-threatening injury and consent given, preserve clothing and body evidence (no washing/toileting), supply emotional support with limited personnel, and coordinate police escort while recording officers’ details.

nodes.title: 성폭행
nodes.summary:
The excerpt is the Korean national “Special-situation Emergency Care Standard Guideline” for sexual-assault victims.  
It defines sexual violence, then gives field-care protocols: minimal, non-blaming history; preservation of clothing and body evidence; psychological support; same-gender crew preference; police notification and chain-of-custody for belongings; indications for on-line medical direction; and mandatory transport to a facility equipped with a sexual-assault evidence kit (Sunflower/One-Stop Center).  
A comprehensive nationwide list of 39 Sunflower Centers (addresses, host hospitals, phone/fax, web/email) is appended for adult and child victims.

nodes.title: 범죄현장
nodes.summary:
The excerpt is the “Special-Situation Emergency Care Standard Guideline” for Korean EMS teams.  
It covers two scenarios:

1. Crime-scene calls  
   – Patient assessment follows normal protocols, but crew and bystander safety is paramount.  
   – If police are absent, notify the station and record arrival time/officer details.  
   – Critical patients are transported immediately without waiting for police; non-critical or uncooperative patients may be held until police arrive and can apply restraint.  
   – Preserve the scene unless life-saving care requires disturbance; document any unavoidable alterations.  
   – Hospital choice is identical to routine cases: nearest appropriate emergency center for severe patients, nearest local facility for minor cases.

2. Patient restraint  
   – Physical restraint by EMS is prohibited; request police assistance.  
   – Evaluate for medical causes of aggression (post-ictal, hypoglycemia, hypoxia, TBI, intoxication, etc.).  
   – Use verbal de-escalation first: calm tone, no threats, avoid direct eye contact, respect personal space, keep exit routes clear, call for backup early.  
   – If physical restraint is required, police must apply soft (cloth) or hard (plastic/leather) devices; EMS documents officer identity and time.

nodes.title: 환자 신체구속(Restraint)
nodes.summary:
The excerpt presents Korean emergency-care guidelines for two “special situations”: (1) patient physical restraint and (2) flood/water-disaster response.  
For restraint, it stresses that Korean EMTs may not legally apply physical or chemical restraints; police must be present, the least-invasive method must be chosen, and continuous monitoring of airway, breathing, circulation, and dignity is mandatory.  
For flood disasters, it highlights rapidly changing hazards, difficult access and location of victims, equipment water-damage risks, prolonged operations, and the need for scene-safety assessment, protective gear, pre-arrival information gathering, and coordinated rescue logistics.

nodes.title: 풍수해
nodes.summary:
The excerpt is the “Flood & Water-Disaster” chapter of Korea’s national “Special-Circumstance Emergency-Care Standard Guideline” for 119 paramedics.  
It explains why climate-driven flash floods are straining rescue capacity, then gives field rules:  
- pre-departure information gathering and protective gear,  
- safe vehicle positioning and hazard recon on arrival,  
- 2-person teams, waterproofing of gear, and communication fall-backs,  
- specific first-aid for trauma, drowning, hypothermia, lightning,  
- criteria for calling on-line medical control or extra fire-service resources.

nodes.title: Ⅵ. 술기 지침
nodes.summary: The excerpt is a field-triage protocol for Korean EMTs. It stresses rapid life-threat assessment, divides patient evaluation into primary (immediate threats) and secondary (detailed) phases, and mandates on-scene safety checks, PPE use, and scene-size-up before patient contact.

nodes.title: 1. 환자 초기 평가·처치 표준지침
nodes.summary:
The excerpt is a detailed Korean pre-hospital protocol that teaches paramedics how to perform an orderly “initial assessment & treatment” on any patient.  
Key points covered:

1. Three-step sequence: scene safety → primary survey (ABCDE) with immediate life-saving interventions → secondary survey (head-to-toe exam, history, vital re-checks).  
2. Decision rule: after the 2-minute primary survey, choose either “rapid transport” for critical patients or complete secondary survey on scene for stable ones.  
3. Systematic checklists for airway, breathing, circulation, disability (AVPU, pupils, motor deficit), exposure/hemorrhage control, oxygen delivery devices and flow rates, spinal precautions, and pediatric vs. adult thresholds.  
4. Triage criteria to classify patients as “emergency” (life-threatening) or “non-emergency,” dictating transport priority and on-scene time.  
5. Structured history tools (OPQRST, SAMPLE) and physical exam mnemonics (DCAP-BTLS) tailored for trauma versus medical cases.  
6. Continuous reassessment every 5–15 min to detect deterioration.

nodes.title: 2. 심폐소생술
nodes.summary: The partial document outlines the main topics or key points discussed within the provided excerpt.

nodes.title: 1) 기본인명 소생술(Basic Life Support)
nodes.summary:
The excerpt is a field-care “Skill Guideline” (술기 지침) focused on high-quality cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) performed by Korean paramedics.  
It covers:  
- Purpose and survival benefit of prompt basic life support  
- Indications (unresponsive, apneic/abnormally breathing patients) and clear contraindications (obvious death, DNAR orders, scene danger, etc.)  
- Common complications (rib fractures, lung bleeding, intrathoracic organ injury)  
- Required personal and airway/CPR equipment list  
- Step-by-step on-scene CPR sequence following 2020 guidelines: check responsiveness & breathing, minimum 6–10 min of continuous compressions, airway management choices (BVM vs. supraglottic vs. ETI with ≤2 attempts), compression metrics (100–120 min⁻¹, ≥5 cm depth, full recoil, minimal pauses)  
- Quality-maintenance tactics (feedback devices, no hyper-ventilation)  
- Continued CPR inside the ambulance: crew restraint, single- vs. two-provider ventilation strategies, 15 L·min⁻¹ oxygen, EtCO₂ monitoring ≥20 mmHg, alternative “Straddle” CPR and mechanical devices when space or staff is limited  
- Concurrent tasks: secure IV access without stopping compressions, monitor for ROSC (coughing, movement, breathing, EtCO₂, pulse)  
- Special pediatric considerations and mandatory annual advanced-airway training for paramedics

nodes.title: 2) 기계식 가슴압박을 이용한 심폐소생술
nodes.summary:
The excerpt is a section of the Korean “Field-Emergency-Care Standard Manual for EMTs.”  
It gives step-by-step guidance on adult cardiac-arrest care, focusing on:

1. Continuous monitoring of spontaneous breathing/circulation and securing an IV line without interrupting chest compressions.  
2. Special notes for pediatric patients and the obligation for annual 4-hour advanced airway training.  
3. Indications, contra-indications, possible complications, required equipment, and procedural details for mechanical chest-compression devices (e.g., LUCAS, AutoPulse).  
4. Identical format for automated external defibrillator (AED) use: indications, contra-indications, complications, and pad placement while compressions continue.

nodes.title: 3. 자동심장충격기(AED)
nodes.summary:
The excerpt is the “Automated External Defibrillator (AED)” and “Bag-valve-mask (BVM)” sections of the Korean EMS field-treatment protocol.  
It gives the rationale, indications, contraindications, possible complications, step-by-step technique, rhythm-check timing, pad-placement rules (including special populations), and transport considerations for AED use, followed by indications and clinical role of BVM ventilation.

nodes.title: 4. 기도관리
nodes.summary: The partial document outlines the main topics or key points discussed within the provided text.

nodes.title: 1) 백밸브마스크(Bag-valve mask; BVM)
nodes.summary:
The excerpt is the “Bag-valve-mask ventilation” and “endotracheal intubation” sections of the Korean EMS “Standard First-Aid Guidelines.”  
It states the purpose, indications (respiratory rates/depths, cyanosis, bradycardia, cardiac arrest, GCS ≤ 8, etc.), contraindications (none), possible complications (gastric distension, aspiration, pneumothorax, etc.), recommended mask/tube and bag sizes by age, step-by-step technique (E-C clamp, two-person seal, 1-sec breaths, OPA/NPA adjuncts, Sellick maneuver, ETCO₂/SpO₂ monitoring, target SpO₂ ≥ 94%), and special cautions for beards, dentures, obesity, pregnancy, and suspected spinal injury.

nodes.title: 2) 기관내 삽관
nodes.summary:
The excerpt is a field-care “Skill Guideline” (Ⅵ) for two advanced airway techniques—endotracheal intubation and the supraglottic airway device I-gel—intended for Korean 1st-class emergency medical technicians.  
For endotracheal intubation it lists: indications (cardiac/respiratory arrest, severe dyspnea, ineffective BVM, GCS ≤ 8, deteriorating consciousness), no absolute contraindications, possible complications (esophageal intubation, airway trauma, pneumothorax, raised ICP, etc.), recommended tube sizes for neonates through adults, step-by-step procedure (pre-oxygenation, equipment check, laryngoscopy, tube insertion depth, cuff inflation, bilateral chest auscultation, ETCO₂ use, fixation with commercial holder or tape), key precautions (≤ 30 s per attempt, max 2 attempts, maintain SpO₂, chest compressions uninterrupted, prepare rescue technique), and pediatric considerations (insertion length = tube size × 3 cm, rapid desaturation).  
For the I-gel it gives: indications (same as above plus failed intubation), contraindications (pharyngeal stenosis or mass), and main risks (aspiration, dislodgement).

nodes.title: 3) 성문 상 기도기：I-gel
nodes.summary: The excerpt is a field-emergency-care manual section for Korean EMTs on two supraglottic airway devices: I-gel and laryngeal mask airway (LMA). It lists indications, contraindications, complications, recommended sizes by age/weight, step-by-step insertion technique, fixation method, and key precautions (max 30 s insertion, continuous SpO₂/ETCO₂ monitoring, readiness for rescue airway or transport).

nodes.title: 4) 성문 상 기도기：후두 마스크(Laryngeal Mask Airway)
nodes.summary:
The excerpt is a field-emergency protocol for Korean EMTs covering:
- Rapid (<30 s) endotracheal intubation precautions (O₂ sat monitoring, back-up plan, tube-position checks).
- Laryngeal Mask Airway (LMA): indications (cardiac/respiratory arrest, severe dyspnea, failed BVM, GCS ≤8, declining consciousness, failed intubation), contraindications (oropharyngeal pathology), and complications (displacement, inadvertent intubation, aspiration, oral injury).
- LMA size–selection table by weight and cuff-inflation volumes.
- Step-by-step LMA insertion technique: pre-oxygenation, equipment list, cuff testing/deflation/lubrication, head-extension/pencil-grip insertion, cuff inflation, leak check, fixation with holder or crisscross tape, and ongoing ventilation assessment every 5–15 min.
- Re-emphasis on 30-s limit, continuous O₂ sat, cuff-pressure risks, and readiness for transfer if airway fails.
- Brief mention of King LTS-D as a dual-cuff esophageal ventilation alternative.

nodes.title: 5) 성문 상 기도기：King LTS-D 삽입
nodes.summary:
The excerpt is a field-emergency airway-management protocol for Korean EMT-paramedics.  
It gives step-by-step instructions for inserting and securing three supraglottic airway devices (King LTS-D, Combitube-equivalent, and Cobra PeriLaryngeal Airway), including sizing, cuff-inflation volumes, pre-oxygenation, insertion angles, fixation with tape/bite-block, and continuous confirmation of placement via auscultation and ETCO₂.  
Key warnings: complete the intubation attempt within 30 s, never interrupt oxygen saturation monitoring, avoid over-inflating cuffs, always have a rescue/transport back-up plan, and recheck tube position every 5–15 min.

nodes.title: 6) 성문 상 기도기：Cobra PeriLaryngeal airway(CPLA)
nodes.summary: The excerpt is a clinical skills guideline (Part 3 Ⅵ) that details step-by-step procedures, precautions, sizing charts and fixation techniques for two advanced airway devices: endotracheal intubation and the Cobra Peri-Laryngeal Airway (CPLA). It also briefly introduces CPAP for oxygen delivery. Key points covered are: proper tape-wrapping sequence to secure an ET tube, timing limits (<30 s), continuous SpO₂ monitoring, cuff-inflation warnings, readiness for rescue/transfer, CPLA indications/contraindications, recommended sizes/cuff volumes by patient weight, insertion technique without laryngoscopy, leak check and fixation using either commercial holder or the same two-tape method, plus identical cautions on cuff pressure and tube position during transport.

nodes.title: 7) 지속적양압환기(CPAP: Continuous positive airway pressure) 산소공급용 지속적양압환기(CPAP) ☞ ①
nodes.summary:
The excerpt is a field-care “skill guideline” (술기 지침) for Korean EMTs.  
It gives step-by-step instructions for two airway/ventilation procedures:

1. Endotracheal intubation – head position, tube insertion to the point of resistance, cuff inflation with specified volume, leak check (auscultation / ETCO₂), tube fixation with commercial holder or crossed tape, and safety limits (≤30 s, monitor SpO₂, avoid over-inflation, have back-up ready).

2. Boussignac CPAP – indications (e.g., pulmonary edema, COPD, post-extubation), contraindications (apnea, pneumothorax, shock, vomiting), side-effects (gastric distension, ↓cardiac output), mask sizing, oxygen flow vs. PEEP table (10 L ≈ 2.5–3 cmH₂O, 15 L ≈ 4.5–5 cmH₂O), assembly sequence, mask seal check, and ongoing vigilance for gastric insufflation.

A short addendum lists six alternative ventilation devices (mouth-to-mask, BVM, demand valve, automatic transport ventilator, etc.) with their indications (apnea, agonal breathing, inadequate ventilation), contraindications (obstructed airway, massive vomitus), and possible complications (barotrauma, abdominal distension, dry mouth).

nodes.title: 5. 양압 환기와 보조환기술식(인공 호흡)
nodes.summary:
The excerpt is a field-EMS “skill guideline” (술기 지침) covering two linked interventions:

1. Positive-pressure & assisted ventilation (인공 호흡)  
   - Definition and urgency (irreversible brain damage in 4–6 min).  
   - Six devices ranked by preference: mouth-to-face-shield, mouth-to-mask with one-way valve, bag-valve mask, demand-valve, portable automatic ventilator, and transtracheal ventilation via existing stoma.  
   - Clear indications (apnea, agonal breathing, inadequate ventilation) and contraindications (obstructed airway, massive upper-airway contamination).  
   - Possible complications: barotrauma, gastric insufflation, oral dryness, skin necrosis under mask.  
   - Step-by-step protocols for each device, including infection control, assembly, mask seal, ventilation rate (10–12 min⁻¹), volume targets (adult 500–1 000 mL), observation of chest rise, and troubleshooting tips.  
   - Special paediatric cautions: use child-size bag, avoid pressure on tracheal tissues, pad torso to accommodate large occiput, do not use demand-valve on small children.

2. Oxygen administration (산소 투여)  
   - Goal: prevent cellular hypoxia and anaerobic metabolism.  
   - Four essential components: oxygen source, regulator/flowmeter, tubing, delivery interface.  
   - Indications: hypoxaemia, increased work of breathing, systemic hypoperfusion/shock, major trauma.  
   - Contraindication: patient who cannot maintain minute ventilation (needs ventilation, not just O₂).  
   - Risks: oxygen toxicity, absorptive atelectasis, respiratory depression, fire hazard.  
   - Devices mentioned: nasal cannula for low-flow requirements.

Overall, the text is a concise, equipment-specific, step-wise manual for pre-hospital airway management and oxygen delivery, with safety checks and paediatric modifications highlighted.

nodes.title: 6. 산소 투여 ☞ ② ①
nodes.summary:
The excerpt is a field-treatment protocol (Part 3 Ⅵ) that explains, step-by-step, how emergency crews should give oxygen and nebulised drugs.

Main points:

1. Oxygen therapy  
   - Purpose: prevent tissue death by supplying > 21 % O₂ to hypoxic patients.  
   - Mandatory 4-piece set-up: O₂ source, regulator/flowmeter, tubing, delivery device.  
   - Indications: hypoxaemia, ↑ work of breathing, shock, major trauma.  
   - Contra-indication: apnoea – needs ventilatory support, not O₂ alone.  
   - Risks: O₂ toxicity, absorptive atelectasis, respiratory depression, fire.  
   - Devices compared (flow rates and resulting FiO₂): nasal cannula, Venturi, simple, partial-rebreather, non-rebreather masks.  
   - Practical procedure: infection control, tank-pressure check, device selection, correct flow, secure fit, monitor bag collapse.  
   - Tank-duration formula provided.  
   - Target SpO₂ ranges for specific adult emergencies (e.g. 94–98 % for most, 88–92 % for COPD, 100 % for CO poisoning, etc.).

2. Nebuliser therapy  
   - Converts liquid drug to aerosol for deep lung deposition.  
   - Indications: COPD exacerbation, asthma.  
   - Contra-indications: drug allergy, uncooperative unconscious patient.  
   - Risks: arrhythmia, allergic reaction.  
   - Procedure: assemble O₂-driven nebuliser (6–10 L/min) or CPAP-compatible set-up; run until medication spent; monitor patient response.

nodes.title: 7. 네뷸라이저 (Nebulizer)
nodes.summary:
The excerpt is a clinical skill-guideline (술기 지침) for aerosol drug delivery via nebulizer and metered-dose inhaler (MDI).  
It lists indications (COPD exacerbation, asthma) and contraindications (drug allergy, altered mental status), summarizes potential adverse effects (arrhythmia, allergic reaction), then gives step-by-step procedures for:  
1) standard nebulizer setup with oxygen 6–10 L/min,  
2) nebulizer combined with Boussignac CPAP at 15 L/min, and  
3) correct MDI technique including shake, exhale, coordinate spray with slow inhalation, breath-hold, and timing between puffs.

nodes.title: 8. 정맥 내 약물투여:말초 정맥로 확보 ☞ ①
nodes.summary:
Part 3 Ⅵ details two pre-hospital skills for EMTs:  
1) Peripheral IV access – indications/contraindications, complications, supplies, step-by-step technique (vein selection, tourniquet, asepsis, catheter insertion, connection, fixation), flow-rate formulas, safety caveats (avoid trauma/infection sites, upper-before-lower extremity, don’t delay transport).  
2) Spinal motion restriction – apply if any loss of consciousness, high-risk mechanism, spine pain/tenderness, neurological deficit or possible intoxication; list possible skin/vomiting risks; describe sizing and application of spinal board, straps and rigid cervical collar.

nodes.title: 9. 척추 고정 (척추 움직임 제한) ☞ ② ①
nodes.summary:
The excerpt is a field-protocol chapter on spinal immobilisation and basic wound care for Korean EMTs.  
It lists clear indications (altered consciousness, high-risk trauma mechanism, mid-spine pain/tenderness, neurologic deficit) and contraindications for spine-board use, details step-by-step application of a cervical collar, long backboard and KED extrication device, warns of pressure sores or aspiration risks, and gives special notes for helmeted, elderly or paediatric patients.  
A short subsequent section covers standard haemorrhage control: elevate, direct sterile pressure, saline rinse, sterile dressing, spiral bandaging from distal to proximal with 50 % overlap, confirm distal circulation/sensation, monitor for re-bleeding during transport.

nodes.title: 10. 손상 처치
nodes.summary: The excerpt is a field-treatment protocol (Standard Guideline 504) for paramedics on “Hemorrhage Control & Wound Dressing.” It lists indications (open wounds), possible complications (bleeding, infection), and a step-by-step procedure: don PPE, elevate/bleed control with sterile gauze pressure, irrigate with saline, cover with sterile gauze, apply elastic bandage from distal-to-proximal with 50 % overlap and no circulatory compromise, check distal pulse/motor/sensation, and monitor for re-bleeding during transport.

nodes.title: 1) 지혈 및 상처 드레싱
nodes.summary:

1) Standard bleeding control and sterile dressing of open wounds – including elevation, direct pressure, irrigation, bandaging rules (distal-to-proximal, 50 % overlap, avoid circulatory compromise) and mandatory distal pulse check.  
2) Management of amputated parts – rinse with saline, wrap in moist (not wet) gauze, seal in a watertight container, cool in ice-water slurry without direct ice contact to prevent tissue necrosis.

nodes.title: 2) 외상 처치: 절단된 조직
nodes.summary:
The excerpt is a clinical-skills guideline (Part 3, Section Ⅵ) on managing amputated tissue.  
Main points:  
- General wound-care precautions: check peripheral pulse after dressing, leave embedded foreign bodies in place, avoid aggressive field cleaning of hard-to-control bleeding, elevate the injured part unless contraindicated.  
- Step-by-step protocol for handling an amputated part: control bleeding at the stump, rinse the severed tissue with normal saline, wrap it in saline-moistened, wrung-out gauze, place the wrapped tissue in a sealed container, and keep the container cooled in ice water or an ice pack without letting the tissue freeze.  
- Indication: any amputated tissue or stump wound; no absolute contraindications.  
- Potential complications: wound infection, bleeding.

nodes.summary:
The excerpt is a field-treatment protocol (Part 3 Ⅵ) on pelvic stabilization.  
Main points:  
- Purpose: quickly stabilize a fractured/unstable pelvis and limit internal bleeding in trauma.  
- Indications: suspected/confirmed pelvic fracture, pelvic instability, internal bleeding signs, high-energy trauma.  
- Contraindications: stable pelvis without fracture, no pelvic trauma, or life-threatening extrapelvic injuries that preclude fixation.  
- Step-by-step procedure: assess circulation/neuro status, inspect/palpate pelvis once, internally rotate lower limbs, center binder over greater trochanters, apply commercial pelvic binder or improvised sheet, avoid excessive force, remove clothing/pockets first, monitor vitals and neuro status continuously, establish IV access early, do not use in pregnancy.  
- Possible complications: increased bleeding, nerve damage, infection, injury to intrapelvic organs.

nodes.title: 6) 외상 처치: 안구손상
nodes.summary:

Main points:  
- Indications: chemical or foreign-body eye injuries  
- No contraindications  
- Risks: infection, further ocular damage  
- Technique: position the eye downward, irrigate with 1–2 L normal saline using gravity until clear, apply bilateral eye pads if painful eye movement  
- Key cautions: chemical injuries are emergencies—do not delay care for vision testing; seek medical direction if unsure

nodes.title: 11. 환자 감시
nodes.summary: The excerpt is a field-treatment guideline for paramedics on monitoring end-tidal CO₂ (EtCO₂). It explains that portable EtCO₂ detectors now allow non-invasive, real-time assessment of ventilation and perfusion. The text lists indications (confirming and monitoring endotracheal-tube position, evaluating CPR effectiveness), contraindications (cannot detect main-stem intubation or be used with mouth-to-tube ventilation), notes no significant side-effects, and distinguishes between quantitative devices: capnometry (numeric display) and capnography (continuous waveform).

nodes.title: 1) 호기말 이산화탄소의 감시
nodes.summary:
The excerpt is a section of the Korean “Field-Emergency-Care Standard Manual for Paramedics.”  
It gives detailed, step-by-step guidance on two topics:

1. End-tidal CO₂ monitoring  
   - Why it is done: confirm and continuously check endotracheal-tube position, monitor CPR effectiveness.  
   - Devices: qualitative colorimetric detectors vs. quantitative capnometry/capnography.  
   - Procedure: intubate → six ventilations → attach detector → interpret numeric/graphic values → troubleshoot mal-positioning or re-intubate if readings are unclear.  
   - Pitfalls: false positives after carbonated drinks or gastric distension, false negatives if tested before six breaths, need for pediatric adapters <15 kg.

2. Personal Protective Equipment in CBRN (Chemical, Biological, Radiological, Nuclear) incidents  
   - Scene safety: recognize hazard, report to designated control agencies, do not enter hot zone.  
   - Indications: patients contaminated with chemical warfare agents, biological terror agents (anthrax, smallpox, plague, etc.), or radioactive materials.  
   - Requirement: all responding paramedics must don appropriate level of PPE to prevent self-contamination.

nodes.title: 12. 개인보호장비
nodes.summary:
The excerpt is a CBRN (chemical-biological-radiological-nuclear) personal-protective-equipment guideline for Korean EMS personnel.  
It stresses that crews must first recognize a CBRN incident, avoid the hot zone, and notify the appropriate national control center (Chemical Safety Center, KCDC, or Nuclear Safety HQ).  
All rescuers must wear situation-specific PPE while performing decontamination.  
The text lists indications for PPE use: patients exposed to chemical warfare agents (nerve, blister, choking, irritant, incapacitating), biological terror agents (anthrax, smallpox, plague, botulinum, tularaemia), or unintended radiation/radioactive contamination.

nodes.title: 1) 화학, 생물학, 방사선 재난상황에서의 개인보호장비
nodes.summary:
The excerpt is a field-first-aid manual section on personal protective equipment (PPE) and emergency childbirth.  
Main points:

1. CBRN (chemical, biological, radiological) incidents  
   – First responders must recognize the hazard, report to the designated national control centre, and stay out of the hot zone until authorized.  
   – Every rescuer must wear situation-appropriate PPE; victims are presumed contaminated until proven otherwise.  
   – Detailed Level-C ensemble lists and step-by-step donning sequences are given for chemical and radiological events, including taping seams, double gloving, and use of personal dosimeters.

2. Emergency delivery outside hospital  
   – Indication: visible crowning.  
   – Risks: post-partum haemorrhage, infection, shock, neonatal hypoxia/infection, maternal or foetal death.  
   – Procedure: sterile gown, gloves, mask, shoe covers, betadine, bulb syringe, clamps/scissors, warm towel; position mother supine with hips and knees flexed.

nodes.title: 13. 응급 분만
nodes.summary:
The excerpt is the “Emergency Childbirth” section of the Korean EMT field-treatment protocol.  
It states the purpose (safe delivery outside hospital), indications (crowning), possible complications (bleeding, infection, shock, neonatal hypoxia, death), and gives a step-by-step sterile technique for normal vertex delivery: positioning, disinfection, controlled head delivery (Ritgen), shoulder delivery, cord management (double-clamp & cut ≥1 min after birth), placental delivery with uterine massage, and immediate neonatal assessment using the APGAR score.  
It also covers abnormal presentations (breech, face, hand) – “transport immediately” – and lists key precautions: prevent newborn falls, keep baby below placenta level until cord clamped, avoid deep suction, no vaginal packing for post-partum bleeding, define significant hemorrhage (>1000 mL or >500 mL with symptoms), and transport if face is already delivered on arrival.

nodes.title: Ⅶ. 약물 지침

nodes.title: 1. Dextrose (포도당주사액)
nodes.summary:

2. Nitroglycerin sublingual tablets – classified as a vasodilator; mechanism of peripheral venous/arterial and coronary dilation to reduce preload/afterload and improve collateral flow; indicated for angina and congestive heart failure; extensive contraindication list (hypotension, bradycardia/tachycardia, recent PDE-5 inhibitor use, glaucoma, anaemia, head trauma, suspected right ventricular infarction); common adverse effects across circulatory, CNS, GI and other systems.

nodes.title: 2. Nitroglycerin(니트로글리세린설하정)
nodes.summary:

It summarizes the drug’s vasodilating mechanism (preload ↓, afterload ↓, collateral coronary flow ↑), classifies it as a vasodilator, lists indications (angina, congestive heart failure), absolute contraindications (hypotension, bradycardia/tachycardia, recent PDE-5 inhibitors, glaucoma, anemia, suspected RV infarction), common adverse effects (headache, flushing, orthostatic hypotension, nausea), formulation/dosing (0.3–0.6 mg SL, max 3 doses 5 min apart), on-scene precautions (sit before dose, check BP before/after), pharmacokinetics (onset 1–3 min, peak 20–45 min, duration 30–60 min), and references.

nodes.title: 3. Normal Saline(생리식염수)

2. Antihistamines

nodes.title: 4. 항히스타민제

nodes.title: 5. Epinephrine(에피네프린)

nodes.title: 7. 비마약성 진통제(진통용)

   – Acetaminophen: indications (fever, mild-moderate pain), cautions/contraindications (hepatic/renal disease, aspirin-asthma, warfarin, alcohol, pregnancy, etc.), serious skin reactions, overdose hepatotoxicity, pharmacokinetics, and IV premix formulation (1000 mg/100 mL, 15-min infusion, onset 5–10 min, duration 4–6 h).

2. Inhaled/nebulized bronchodilators

nodes.title: 8. 기관지 확장제(흡입용/분무용)

nodes.title: 9. 정질용액(플라스마솔루션/하트만솔루션)

nodes.title: 3. 구급상황센터 의료상담에 필요한 의학용어 정리

nodes.summary: The excerpt is a quick-reference glossary for EMS crews: it lists the medical terms, Korean names, and common abbreviations for hospital departments (Internal Medicine, Surgery, etc.) and inpatient units (ER, ICU, OR, GW) that dispatchers or paramedics may encounter when consulting the emergency medical call center.

nodes.summary: The excerpt is a bilingual (Korean-English) glossary of symptom-related medical terms intended for use in emergency run sheets. It groups common complaints alphabetically by English keyword, gives the Korean translation, and covers cardinal symptoms from every body system—neurologic, respiratory, cardiovascular, gastrointestinal, genitourinary, musculoskeletal, dermatologic, and general—providing paramedics with a quick on-scene vocabulary reference.

nodes.summary:
The excerpt is a bilingual (Korean-English) appendix that lists two groups of emergency-medicine terms with their abbreviations and Korean translations.
